introduction: How is a new civilization to be built? The guide answers with means: a parliament of nations, a common auxiliary language, just law, education, organised work for peace, and beneath them a change of heart and a framework of administration that it holds to be new in kind. Its forty-three quotations, many of them from letters written for the Bahá’í community in the twentieth century, are read here with forty-three from elsewhere. The prophets’ visions of swords beaten into plowshares and of the wolf with the lamb, Tennyson’s parliament of man, Hugo’s united Europe, Zamenhof’s case for a shared language, Garrison’s motto and the constitution of UNESCO are the older and wider forms of the same hope. Kant’s fear of a universal monarchy, Madison’s reminder that institutions are needed because people are not angels, Douglass on agitation, Burke on the value of what is old, Samuel’s warning about kings, the Preacher’s doubt that anything is new and Lao Tzu’s small contented state are set where the guide’s confidence in a new order is strongest. Augustine’s two cities stand at the end, beside the promise of a world civilization.
questions: The guide lists practical means of a peaceful world: a parliament of nations, a common language, education, law. Which seems to you furthest from being realised, and why?
Kant feared a world government as much as he hoped for peace. What safeguards would a federation of nations need?
Madison says institutions exist because people are not angels, and the guide says a change of heart is needed. Which must come first, and can either come without the other?
The story of Babel treats one language as a danger and Zephaniah treats it as a promise. What would a common language have to be for the second to be true?
The guide says its administrative order is different from any existing system and yet does not belittle them. How can a community hold both attitudes?
All must take part, however limited their means. What is the smallest contribution to such a civilization that you could begin now?

outside.why: Revelation hears the one who sat upon the throne say: behold, I make all things new.
Isaiah foresees nations that beat their swords into plowshares and do not learn war any more.
Tennyson's phrase for it was the Parliament of man, the Federation of the world, where the battle-flags are furled.
Kant preferred a federation of separate states to their fusion into a universal monarchy by one power that has overgrown the rest. What keeps a parliament of nations from becoming that?
Zamenhof argued that if we had but two languages to learn we should know them far better, and that difference of speech is a cause of antipathy between people.
Zephaniah promises that the peoples will be turned to a pure language, to serve with one consent.
In Genesis one language made a people able to do whatever they imagined, and it was confounded. What does that story warn of in any plan for a common tongue?
Aristotle held that whoever bids the law rule bids God and Reason alone rule.
Madison wrote that if men were angels no government would be necessary, and that government is the greatest of all reflections on human nature. Does a new order need new institutions, or new people?
Garrison's motto was: our country is the world, our countrymen are mankind.
Victor Hugo told the nations of Europe that a day would come when they would be joined without losing their distinctive qualities.
Jesus blesses the peacemakers, and says that they shall be called the children of God.
Jesus tells a follower to put up his sword, for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
Douglass said that those who favour freedom and deprecate agitation want crops without plowing up the ground. How far can a just cause go in pressing its claim?
UNESCO's constitution holds that since wars begin in the minds of men, the defences of peace must be constructed there.
Tennyson's bells ring out the old and ring in the new, ring out the false and ring in the true.
Burke said that his countrymen cherish their old prejudices the more for having lasted long. Is every old thought fit for the scrap-heap after a war?
The Qur'an says that God does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in their hearts.
Proverbs puts the building of the future in the nursery: train up a child in the way he should go.
Yeats wrote of such a time that things fall apart and the centre cannot hold.
John sees a new heaven and a new earth, the first heaven and the first earth having passed away.
Paul describes his own work as laying a foundation, as a wise masterbuilder, on which others build.
Ezekiel promises a new heart and a new spirit in place of the heart of stone.
Paul asks his readers not to be conformed to this world but transformed by the renewing of their mind.
Acts says that God has made of one blood all nations of men to dwell on all the face of the earth.
Malachi asks: have we not all one father? hath not one God created us?
Jesus separates what is to be rendered to Caesar from what is to be rendered to God.
Pericles praised a city in which ordinary citizens are fair judges of public matters, and one who takes no part is thought useless.
Aristotle thought the best political community avoided extremes, being formed by citizens of the middle class.
Jesus says that new wine is put into new bottles, and both are preserved.
The Preacher holds that there is no new thing under the sun. What would count as evidence that a form of order is really new?
Samuel warns a people who ask for a king that they will become his servants and cry out in that day. What does any people give up when it accepts a new form of authority?
Jesus likens the kingdom to a mustard seed, the least of seeds, which becomes the greatest among herbs.
Jesus warns his own followers that salt which has lost its savour is good for nothing.
Shelley, among the poets, sang that the world's great age begins anew and the golden years return.
Isaiah, among the seers, saw the wolf dwelling with the lamb and the leopard lying down with the kid.
Lao Tzu's vision of peace is a small state whose people never visit their neighbours. Is the Great Peace one world joined together, or many places left alone?
Paul tells each to use the gift given, whether prophecy, ministry, teaching or giving.
Jesus says that the harvest truly is great, but the labourers are few.
Habakkuk foresees an earth filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea.
Whitman saw God's purpose in the earth spanned and the lands welded together.
Micah's picture of the civilization to come is each one sitting under his vine and fig tree, with none to make them afraid.
Augustine says two cities have been formed by two loves, the earthly by the love of self and the heavenly by the love of God. Can the heavenly city be built in history, or only journeyed toward?
